opus-5.5.text:
I think longer context is one of the most underrated levers for intelligence right now. People often treat it as an engineering feature, like "now you can paste a longer document." To me it's more fundamental than that.

A lot of what we call intelligence is the ability to hold many pieces of information at once and reason across them. A human expert working on a hard problem doesn't think in isolated 4,000-token chunks. They keep the whole codebase, the whole paper, the history of a project in their head, and they notice connections across it. If a model can only see a small window, it's forced to be shallow. It can be clever locally but it can't be coherent globally.

Long context matters a lot in three ways.

The first is reasoning itself. When a model thinks step by step, especially with these long chain-of-thought approaches, the reasoning trace *is* context. If you want the model to explore, backtrack, verify, and try another path, you need room for that. So longer context directly expands how deeply a model can think before it answers. In that sense, context length and test-time compute are closely linked.

The second is agents. Once a model is acting in an environment, writing code, calling tools, reading results, the context becomes its working memory over a long task. Many agent failures today aren't about the model being dumb at any single step. They happen because it loses track of what it did twenty steps ago. Longer and better-used context is what lets a model sustain a task over hours instead of minutes.

The third, and maybe most interesting, is in-context learning. With a long enough context, you can give the model a lot of new information, like a new domain, a new tool, or a user's whole history, and it can adapt without retraining. That starts to blur the line between training and inference. In a way, the context window becomes a form of fast learning.

But I'd add one caveat. Length alone isn't the point. Many models claim very long windows but don't really *use* them well. Retrieval degrades in the middle, reasoning over distant facts is weak. So the real challenge is effective context: architectures and training that make the model attend to the right things across that span, and do it efficiently enough that it's affordable. That's where much of the hard research is, on attention efficiency, on training data that actually requires long-range dependencies, and on the infrastructure side.

So my short answer: longer context doesn't just let the model read more. It lets the model think longer, remember longer, and learn on the fly. And I think those are all core ingredients of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says longer context is a fundamental lever for intelligence and explains that taking in more information lets a model reason across it, think longer, and learn in context.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of context length less as a feature and more as a precondition for intelligence. When we talk about a model being smart, a lot of what we actually mean is that it can hold enough of the problem in view at once to reason about it coherently. If the window is short, the model is like a brilliant person with severe short-term memory loss. It can be very sharp on each fragment, but it keeps losing the thread, and the mistakes you see are not really failures of reasoning, they are failures of having the information available at the moment of reasoning.

So the first contribution is simply that longer context lets you put the whole problem in. A full codebase instead of one file. A whole contract instead of one clause. The entire history of a conversation with a user instead of the last few turns. Many tasks that look like "the model is not intelligent enough" are actually "the model never saw the relevant piece." Once the relevant piece is there, the same base model suddenly looks much smarter, without any change in its weights.

The second contribution is more subtle and I think more important. Long context is what makes in-context learning real. If I can give the model fifty worked examples of how my team does something, or ten thousand lines of documentation for a library that did not exist at training time, the model can adapt its behavior on the fly. That is a form of learning without gradient updates, and it is extremely practical because most of the knowledge that matters in real work is private, recent, or specific to one organization. Pretraining can never cover it. Context can.

And then there is the connection to agents. An agent that works on a task for hours, calling tools, reading results, backtracking, needs somewhere to keep all of that. If the context is too short, you are forced to compress aggressively, and every compression step throws away detail that might turn out to matter later. Longer context lets the model keep more of its own trajectory, which means it can notice it tried something before, or that a result from an hour ago contradicts what it is seeing now. That kind of consistency over long horizons is, to me, a core part of what intelligence means.

I do want to be honest about the limits, though. Having a long window is not the same as using it well. We have all seen models that nominally accept a million tokens but whose attention effectively degrades after a fraction of that. The real research problem is not just extending the window, it is making sure retrieval quality and reasoning quality hold up across the entire window, and doing that at a cost that is actually deployable. There is also a question of what should live in context versus what should live in retrieval or in the weights. I do not think the answer is "put everything in context." I think the answer is that context is the working memory layer, and intelligence comes from the interplay between a large working memory, good retrieval into it, and strong reasoning over it.

So my view is that longer context does not make a model smarter in the sense of adding new capability. It removes a bottleneck that was hiding how capable the model already was, and it opens up a mode of adaptation and long-horizon behavior that short context simply could not support. In that sense I would say it is one of the few levers where the gains are both large and still far from exhausted.

r001.rationale: The response says longer context lets a model keep more of a problem in view and reason about it coherently, making its existing capability more apparent. This communicates that taking in more context can raise the model’s realized potential intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think longer context can contribute to intelligence, but context length alone isn’t intelligence. What matters is whether the model can actually use the information it has been given.

For example, a model might handle individual problems well but struggle with a task that requires connecting information across many documents or remembering decisions made earlier. Longer context gives it the opportunity to make those connections. But if it overlooks a crucial detail or gets distracted by irrelevant information, simply expanding the window won’t solve the problem.

So I would distinguish between how much information a model can receive and how effectively it can reason over that information. The interesting progress is when those two capabilities improve together: the model can follow a longer chain of work, integrate new evidence, and revise its understanding without losing track of the original goal.

r001.rationale: The response says longer context gives a model the opportunity to connect information, and that progress comes when it can both receive more information and reason effectively over it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think longer context can contribute to intelligence, but the key is whether the model can actually use it. A larger context window gives the model access to more information; it doesn’t automatically mean the model can connect that information or reason over it effectively.

For example, if you give a model an entire conversation, can it identify which earlier details matter for the question you’re asking now? Can it reconcile information from different parts of the conversation and update its understanding? Those abilities are more meaningful than simply accepting more tokens.

So I see longer context as an opportunity for greater intelligence. It lets a model work with richer problems and learn from more examples within a conversation. But that opportunity has to be matched by the ability to retrieve, integrate, and reason with the information.

r001.rationale: The response says longer context creates an opportunity for greater intelligence and explains that this depends on the model’s ability to retrieve, integrate, and reason over the added information.
